Abstract

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a fundamental architecture for graph representation learning through neighborhood aggregation. However, as the number of layers increases,repeated message passing often leads to unstable representation evolution, less discriminative node representations, and degraded performance. Inspired by classical control theory, we introduce a Propor ckktion dynamics of GCNs. The proposed method, termed PIGCN, uses proportional feedback to correct layer-wise propagation discrepancies and integral feedback to aggregate historical correction signals,thereby stabilizing deep graph propagation, preserving discriminative node representations, and improving the performance of deep GCNs. We provide a spectral analysis to theoretically characterize how PI feedback reshapes propagation dynamics. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PIGCN consistently improves multiple representative GCN backbones and achieves superior performance over representative baselines in both accuracy and propagation stability.In particular, our PI-Linear variant achieves 65.15% accuracy on the large-scale Paper-100M benchmark, demonstrating the scalability and effectiveness of our framework on large graphs.

1 Introduction

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a standard paradigm for learning representations from graph-structured data by jointly exploiting node attributes and graph topology [13, 21]. Through recursive neighborhood aggregation, GNNs enlarge the receptive field of each node and capture structural dependencies beyond local features [13]. This message-passing mechanism has achieved strong performance on various graph learning tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph-level prediction.

Despite their success, GNNs remain difficult to scale to large depths. Repeated message passing may make the layer-wise evolution of node representations unstable and progressively less discriminative, leading to degraded trainability and poor generalization [3, 27, 32, 43]. As depth increases, graph propagation repeatedly mixes neighborhood information and may suppress taskrelevant signals, accumulate propagation bias, and drive hidden representations toward less informative states. Such depth-induced degradation can manifest as representation homogenization, lowdimensional feature collapse, or excessive concentration toward dominant spectral components [14, 22, 26, 38].Therefore, regulating the layer-wise evolution of node representations is crucial for improving the stability and discriminability of deep GNNs under repeated message passing

Existing studies have improved deep graph propagation from several perspectives, including residual and identity mappings, normalization and regularization, decoupled propagation, diffusion-based models,and spectral fltering[1,3,6,12,18,24,30,35,39,4].These methods alleviate depth-induced degradation by preserving earlier representations, regulating embedding geometry, aggregating multi-hop signals, or designing frequency-selective filters. However,most existing methods improve deep propagation by redesigning the propagation architecture, normalization strategy, or spectral filter, rather than explicitly controlling how repeated propagation reshapes spectral components across layers. How to regulate the spectral evolution of node representations during deep message passing remains less explored.

Spectral filtering provides an important perspective for understanding depth-induced degradation in graph propagation. Repeated message passing can progressively concentrate node representations toward dominant spectral components, causing nondominant components that may carry discriminative information to decay. Existing spectral GNNs improve this process mainly by designing or learning frequency-selective filters, such as low-pass,high-pass, band-pass, or adaptive polynomial filters [1, 6, 9, 16, 18,20, 39]. However, these methods primarily focus on filter design,while less attention has been paid to regulating the spectral evolution induced by repeated propagation itself. This motivates us to study whether feedback-based propagation control can reshape spectral energy evolution and improve the stability of deep GNNs.

In this work, we propose PIGCN, a feedback-regulated graph propagation framework for improving the stability of deep GNNs.Instead of treating deep graph propagation as a purely feedforward transformation, PIGCN views it as an iterative dynamical process and introduces proportional-integral feedback into layer-wise propagation. The proportional term captures the discrepancy between adjacent propagation states, while the integral term accumulates historical propagation discrepancies along the depth trajectory.Through these feedback signals, PIGCN regulates the propagation dynamics of deep GNNs and reshapes the spectral evolution of node representations, thereby reducing excessive spectral concentration and preserving more discriminative information under repeated message passing. Moreover, PIGCN extends effectively to largescale graphs, maintaining competitive predictive performance with low GPU memory overhead.

Related propagation-based methods,such as APPNP and DAGNN, decouple feature transformation from propagation or adaptively fuse multi-hop representations[12, 2].These methods improve depth robustness mainly by preserving earlier representations or aggregating information across propagation depths.

Another family of methods mitigates over-smoothing through normalization and regularization [30, 32, 43, 44].PairNorm preserves pairwise feature distances to prevent node embeddings from becoming overly similar [43], while DropEdge randomly removes edges during training to reduce excessive neighborhood mixing [30].Recent studies further show that residual connections and normalization layers can prevent complete representation collapse, and GraphNormv2 improves the centering operation to better preserve useful graph signals [2].These approaches mainly regulate representation geometry, feature scale, or graph connectivity.

Spectral filtering provides another important perspective for understanding graph propagation. From this viewpoint, message passing can be interpreted as frequency-selective processing of graph signals, and depth-induced degradation is closely related to how repeated propagation reshapes spectral components. Representative spectral GNNs, such as GPR-GNN, FAGCN, ARMA, BernNet,DSF, and UniFilter, improve graph learning through adaptive propagation weights,frequency-aware filtering, rational filters, polynomial approximations, or homophily-heterophily adaptive spectral responses[1,2, 6, 9,16, 18,20,39].In parallel, dynamical-system approaches model graph propagation through difusion, diferentialequation discretization, or stable graph dynamics [10, 15, 29, 35].These methods provide useful tools for designing propagation operators and understanding deep graph dynamics, but they mainly focus on filter design, propagation formulation, or continuous-depth modeling.

Scaling GNNs to large graphs remains challenging due to the computational and memory costs of message passing. Existing approaches improve scalability through sampling, graph partitioning,sparsification, or coarsening. GraphSAGE uses neighborhood sampling, Cluster-GCN forms mini-batches from graph clusters, and GraphSAINT samples subgraphs for mini-batch training[5, 17, 41].Recent methods also explore graph sparsification and coarsening.SGNN-LS uses Laplacian sparsification to approximate spectral graph propagation with theoretical guarantees [8], while Graph Batch Coarsening reduces computational costs through graph decomposition and coarsening [42]. 3 PI Control for GCN
In this section, we first introduce PIGCN, a PI-controlled graph convolutional network. We then discuss its basic properties and finally present an improved variant with a sparse integral term.
3.1 PI-Controlled GCN
Proportional-Integral (PI) control is a classical feedback mechanism for discrete-time dynamical systems [11, 34]. In the discrete-time setting, a nonlinear control system can be written as

where $x_{k}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{n}$ denotes the system state and $u_{k}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{n}$ denotes the control input. The goal of controller design is to construct a sequence $u_{k}$ that drives xk toward a reference state $x_{k}^{*}$ . Accordingly,we define the tracking error as $e_{k}=x_{k}-x_{k}^{*}$ . A standard PI controller then takes the form
\begin{array}{r l r}{u_{k}}&{{}=}&{-\alpha e_{k}-\beta I_{k},}\end{array}

Here,$e_{k}$ is the proportional term, which provides an immediate correction based on the current error, while $I_{k}\;=\;e_{k}+\gamma I_{k-1}$ is the integral term, which accumulates historical errors to reduce persistent bias.

Motivated by this classical formulation, we next introduce an analogous PI feedback mechanism into graph convolutional propagation. In fact, the general form of a graph convolutional network is described as

4 Experiment
4.1 Experiment Setup

Datasets. We evaluate our method on 10 widely used node classification benchmarks spanning homophilous and heterophilous graphs, and include the large-scale citation graph oGBN-PAPERs100M [19]. Specifically, we use three Planetoid citation networks, including CoRA, CITESEER, and PuBMED [25, 33]; two WebKB graphs,WIscoNSIn and CoRNeLL [7]; two WikipediaNetwork graphs, including SQUIRREL and CHAMELEON [31]. We additionally include the RoMAN-EMPIRE benchmark [28], as well as PENN94 and ARXIvYEAR from the LINKX benchmark suite [23]. We follow the standard splits for Planetoid datasets and use the commonly adopted 10 fixed splits for WebKB and WikipediaNetwork datasets. Detailed dataset statistics are provided in Table 1.

Baselines. To evaluate PI feedback on message-passing backbones, we use GCN [21] and GCNII [3], comparing each with its PI-enhanced counterpart at matched depths and under identical training settings. We also compare PI-enhanced models with re resentative methods for deep graph propagation, over-smoothing mitigation, spectral filtering, and heterophilous graphs. These baselines includeGPR-GNN[6], APPNP [12], DAGNN [24], H2GCN [45],LINKX[23], ARMA[1], BERNET[18],FAGCN[2],DSF [16], and UNIFILTER [20]. We additionally evaluate whether PI complemets established over-smoothing mitigation methods,including PairNorM [43], GRAPHNoRMv2 [32], and DRoEDGE [30].
For large-scale evaluation, we additionally include Simplifying Graph Convolution (SGC) [37] and the Laplacian-sparsification
methods introduced by Ding et al.[8], namely GPR-LS and APPNPLS, sparse variants of GPR-GNN and APPNP, respectively.

Training Details. All methods are evaluated under a unified protocol withthe amedatasplits,traiing budgets,andvaliation-bae model selection. We evaluate depths $L\in\{3,8,16,32\}$ for the main comparison and further include $L\in\{64,128\}$ for deep propagation analysis. We use official or standard splits when available, and otherwise follow commonly used fixed random splits. For strong baselines, we use official implementations and recommended hyperparameter settings whenever available; otherwise, we tune them on the validation set under the same protocol. The additional PI coefficients are also selected by validation performance. The test set is not used for depth, hyperparameter, or checkpoint selection.Results are averaged over multiple random seeds, with test accuracy reported at the checkpoint with the best validation performance.Detailed settings are provided in Appendix B.1.

Evaluation Metrics. We report node classification accuracy as mean ± standard deviation over random runs, using the checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy. To track whether node representations settle as propagation deepens, we report the Relative Layer-wise Change (RLC): decreasing values indicate smaller changes between consecutive layers, and values approaching zero indicate layer-wise convergence. To assess whether this stabilization comes with over-smoothing or loss of representation diversity,we also report PairSim, Dirichlet Energy, and effective rank. PairSim tracks node-wise similarity, Dirichlet Energy measures variation across graph edges (with excessively low values potentially indicating over-smoothing), and effective rank summarizes feature-space diversity. Together, these metrics help distinguish stable propagation that preserves representation differences from stabilization accompanied by homogenization or feature collapse. Their formal definitions and interpretations are provided in Appendix B.1.

5 Conclusion

We proposed PIGCN, a proportional-integral feedback framework for stabilizing deep graph propagation. By correcting current propagation discrepancies and accumulating historical discrepancies,PIGCN regulates the layer-wise evolution of node representations under repeated message passing. Our analysis shows that PI feedback reshapes the effective propagation behavior from a spectral perspective, helping preserve discriminative information in deep GNNs. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and representative backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and compatibility of PIGCN. Propagation analyses further show that PI feedback improves deep stability by alleviating representation homogenization and maintaining stronger performance at larger depths. On the large-scale ogbn-papers100M benchmark, PI-Linear-8 achieves $65.15\pm0.08\%$ accuracy with a peak GPU memory usage of 40.12 GB,demonstrating the feasibility of PI-based propagation on graphs with over 100 million nodes. This feedback-regulated view provides a practical principle forimproving the stability and dicrimiaility of deep graph neural networks.

Abstract

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a fundamental architecture for graph representation learning through neighborhood aggregation. However, as the number of layers increases,repeated message passing often leads to unstable representation evolution, less discriminative node representations, and degraded performance. Inspired by classical control theory, we introduce a Propor ckktion dynamics of GCNs. The proposed method, termed PIGCN, uses proportional feedback to correct layer-wise propagation discrepancies and integral feedback to aggregate historical correction signals,thereby stabilizing deep graph propagation, preserving discriminative node representations, and improving the performance of deep GCNs. We provide a spectral analysis to theoretically characterize how PI feedback reshapes propagation dynamics. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PIGCN consistently improves multiple representative GCN backbones and achieves superior performance over representative baselines in both accuracy and propagation stability.In particular, our PI-Linear variant achieves 65.15% accuracy on the large-scale Paper-100M benchmark, demonstrating the scalability and effectiveness of our framework on large graphs.

1 Introduction

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a standard paradigm for learning representations from graph-structured data by jointly exploiting node attributes and graph topology [13, 21]. Through recursive neighborhood aggregation, GNNs enlarge the receptive field of each node and capture structural dependencies beyond local features [13]. This message-passing mechanism has achieved strong performance on various graph learning tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph-level prediction.

Despite their success, GNNs remain difficult to scale to large depths. Repeated message passing may make the layer-wise evolution of node representations unstable and progressively less discriminative, leading to degraded trainability and poor generalization [3, 27, 32, 43]. As depth increases, graph propagation repeatedly mixes neighborhood information and may suppress taskrelevant signals, accumulate propagation bias, and drive hidden representations toward less informative states. Such depth-induced degradation can manifest as representation homogenization, lowdimensional feature collapse, or excessive concentration toward dominant spectral components [14, 22, 26, 38].Therefore, regulating the layer-wise evolution of node representations is crucial for improving the stability and discriminability of deep GNNs under repeated message passing

Existing studies have improved deep graph propagation from several perspectives, including residual and identity mappings, normalization and regularization, decoupled propagation, diffusion-based models,and spectral fltering[1,3,6,12,18,24,30,35,39,4].These methods alleviate depth-induced degradation by preserving earlier representations, regulating embedding geometry, aggregating multi-hop signals, or designing frequency-selective filters. However,most existing methods improve deep propagation by redesigning the propagation architecture, normalization strategy, or spectral filter, rather than explicitly controlling how repeated propagation reshapes spectral components across layers. How to regulate the spectral evolution of node representations during deep message passing remains less explored.

Spectral filtering provides an important perspective for understanding depth-induced degradation in graph propagation. Repeated message passing can progressively concentrate node representations toward dominant spectral components, causing nondominant components that may carry discriminative information to decay. Existing spectral GNNs improve this process mainly by designing or learning frequency-selective filters, such as low-pass,high-pass, band-pass, or adaptive polynomial filters [1, 6, 9, 16, 18,20, 39]. However, these methods primarily focus on filter design,while less attention has been paid to regulating the spectral evolution induced by repeated propagation itself. This motivates us to study whether feedback-based propagation control can reshape spectral energy evolution and improve the stability of deep GNNs.

In this work, we propose PIGCN, a feedback-regulated graph propagation framework for improving the stability of deep GNNs.Instead of treating deep graph propagation as a purely feedforward transformation, PIGCN views it as an iterative dynamical process and introduces proportional-integral feedback into layer-wise propagation. The proportional term captures the discrepancy between adjacent propagation states, while the integral term accumulates historical propagation discrepancies along the depth trajectory.Through these feedback signals, PIGCN regulates the propagation dynamics of deep GNNs and reshapes the spectral evolution of node representations, thereby reducing excessive spectral concentration and preserving more discriminative information under repeated message passing. Moreover, PIGCN extends effectively to largescale graphs, maintaining competitive predictive performance with low GPU memory overhead.

Evaluation Metrics. We report node classification accuracy as mean ± standard deviation over random runs, using the checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy. 5 Conclusion

We proposed PIGCN, a proportional-integral feedback framework for stabilizing deep graph propagation. By correcting current propagation discrepancies and accumulating historical discrepancies,PIGCN regulates the layer-wise evolution of node representations under repeated message passing. Our analysis shows that PI feedback reshapes the effective propagation behavior from a spectral perspective, helping preserve discriminative information in deep GNNs. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and representative backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and compatibility of PIGCN. Propagation analyses further show that PI feedback improves deep stability by alleviating representation homogenization and maintaining stronger performance at larger depths. On the large-scale ogbn-papers100M benchmark, PI-Linear-8 achieves $65.15\pm0.08\%$ accuracy with a peak GPU memory usage of 40.12 GB,demonstrating the feasibility of PI-based propagation on graphs with over 100 million nodes. This feedback-regulated view provides a practical principle forimproving the stability and dicrimiaility of deep graph neural networks.
